title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Normocytic normochromic anemia is a type of anemia in which the circulating red blood cells (RBCs) are the same size (normocytic) and have a normal red color (normochromic). Most normochromic anemias are secondary to other diseases; a minority reflect a primary disorder of the blood. Management depends primarily on treating the underlying cause of anemia. This activity will focus on the role of the interprofessional team in diagnosing and managing normocytic normochromic anemia.

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Introduction
content: Anemia is a condition marked by a decrease in red blood cells (RBC), the proportion of hemoglobin, or the collective volume of packed RBCs (hematocrit). The main function of RBCs, or erythrocytes, is to carry oxygen from the lungs to the body tissues and carbon dioxide as a waste product from the body tissues to the lungs. This process is facilitated by hemoglobin. A decrease in the number of RBCs transporting oxygen and carbon dioxide in anemia decreases the body’s capacity for proper gas exchange. The impairment may result from blood loss, increased destruction, or reduced production of RBCs. Traditionally, the decrease is quantified by the hematocrit, defined as the ratio of packed RBCs to blood volume, and by hemoglobin concentration. [1] [2]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Introduction
content: Anemia can be classified according to mean corpuscular volume (MCV), a measure of the average volume of RBCs in a specimen. Low MCV indicates microcytic, normal MCV indicates normocytic, and high MCV indicates macrocytic. [3] Anemia is generally defined as hemoglobin of less than 13.0 g/dL in men and less than 12.0 g/dL in premenopausal women. [4] Normocytic normochromic anemia differs from other forms of anemia because the RBCs' average size and hemoglobin content are typically within normal limits. RBCs typically appear similar to normal cells under microscopic examination. In some cases, variations in size and shape may equalize, resulting in average values within the normal range. Normocytic, normochromic anemia most commonly results from various chronic infections and systemic diseases. Most normocytic anemias appear to result from impaired RBC production. [5]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Etiology
content: Most normochromic, normocytic anemias are a consequence of other diseases; a minority reflects a primary disorder of the blood. This may be due to anemia of chronic disease (inflammation, neoplasia), renal failure, endocrine failure (hypothyroidism, hypopituitarism), marrow failure (pure red-cell aplasia, aplastic anemia, infiltration), acute blood loss, and polymyalgia rheumatica. [6] The etiology of normocytic normochromic anemia depends on whether the anemia is hypoproliferative (ie, corrected reticulocyte count <2%) or hyperproliferative (ie, corrected reticulocyte count >2%). [7] [8]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Epidemiology
content: Epidemiologic data are not available for all conditions associated with normocytic normochromic anemia, taking together the most common cause of normocytic normochromic anemia is anemia of chronic disease; a summary by Wiess et al shows the estimated prevalence percentage of underlying causes of anemia of chronic disease (infections 18% to 95%, cancer 30% to 77%, autoimmune 8% to 71%, chronic rejection after solid organ transplantation 8% to 71% and chronic kidney disease and inflammation 23% to 50%. Nevertheless, the prevalence of normocytic normochromic anemia in patients with less common causes like endocrine failure, marrow failure, acute blood loss, etc, is not well defined. [9]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Pathophysiology
content: The pathogenetic mechanisms of normocytic normochromic anemia vary; specifics depend largely on the etiological cause. Several factors contribute to the cumulative cause of anemia. Since chronic disease anemia accounts for a substantial proportion of normocytic normochromic anemia cases and shares common pathophysiology with other causes of normocytic normochromic anemia, in the following section, we focus primarily on the pathways involved in anemia of chronic disease, along with other associated conditions.

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Pathophysiology
content: Anemia of chronic disease (also called anemia of inflammation) is usually a mild-to-moderate normocytic, normochromic anemia; over time, it may evolve to hypochromic and at later stages can microcytic, although usually less microcytic than in iron deficiency. Fewer than 25% of cases of normocytic, normochromic anemia progress to microcytic, hypochromic anemia, and if occuring, mean corpuscular volume is rarely less than 70. [9] [10] The hemoglobin concentration is usually 8 g/dL to 9.5 g/dL (mild to moderate anemia) and rarely drops below 6 g/dL. In cases of severe anemia, other causes of red cell loss or destruction should be strongly considered. Anemia of chronic disease may be secondary to infections, malignancies, autoimmune disorders, or chronic renal failure.

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Pathophysiology
content: Compared to iron-deficient anemia, anemia of chronic disease usually is associated with low-to-normal iron stores, low-to-normal total iron binding capacity (TIBC), elevated ferritin, normal red cell distribution (RDW), normal mean hemoglobin concentration (MCH), and less severe hemoglobin decrease. Similar to iron deficiency, soluble transferring is usually low. Of note, anemia of chronic disease and iron deficiency can coexist, particularly in the setting of malignancy, occult gastrointestinal bleeding, inflamatory bowel disease, autoimmune diseases, and chronic infections. [11] [12] [13] [14]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Pathophysiology
content: The pathophysiology of normocytic normochromic anemia is complex. Still, it typically reflects 3 broad causes, each associated with increased pro-inflammatory cytokines and subsequent hepcidin elevation. In addition, inappropriate erythropoietin (EPO) levels, a diminished erythropoietin response, and reduced RBC survival contribute to normocytic normochromic anemia. This is the underlying mechanism most commonly seen in patients with acute renal failure. [11] [12]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Pathophysiology
content: Increase in Pro-inflammatory Cytokines and Iron Dysregulation: This increase is associated with a variety of disease states, including infection, neoplasms, chronic kidney disease, and autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus. Hepcidin is the main modulator of iron metabolism, which is central to the pathophysiology of chronic disease and anemia. Interleukin-6 (IL-6) and other proinflammatory cytokines facilitate upregulation of the acute-phase protein hepcidin. Hepcidin binds to the iron export protein, ferroportin, in macrophages, hepatocytes, and enterocytes. Increased hepcidin levels lead to iron trapping within macrophages and hepatocytes, resulting in low circulating iron levels. Through negative feedback stimulated by increased iron stores, hepcidin causes enterocytes and macrophages to degrade ferroportin, thus reducing absorption and promoting storage. [15] [16]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Pathophysiology
content: Inappropriate EPO Levels or Less Response to Erythropoietin: In a healthy individual, erythropoietin circulates in the bone marrow to assist in producing RBCs, thereby improving oxygen concentration in the blood and relieving hypoxia. Recent studies have identified numerous cytokines that inhibit hemopoiesis in the bone marrow and contribute to a subnormal erythropoietin response, with the degree of anemia determining the magnitude of these effects. For example, in patients with chronic kidney disease, anemia is primarily due to EPO deficiency. Because kidney function plays an important role in hepcidin clearance, kidney dysfunction reduces hepcidin clearance and leads to its accumulation, resulting in hyposideremic anemia . [17] Several inflammatory proteins and the inflammatory cytokine, especially IL-6, have been linked to this diminished response to erythropoietin. These cytokines downregulate SLC4a1 expression in late erythroid precursors, thereby reducing hemoglobin synthesis. This process results in increased hepatic hepcidin synthesis. [18] [19]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Pathophysiology
content: Decreased RBC Survival and Bone Marrow Infiltration: Several studies have identified a mild shortening of the red-cell lifespan in normocytic normochromic anemia cases, which appears to be due to an extracorpuscular factor or intrinsic abnormality of the red cells. RBC survival is usually not markedly shortened, and marrow function should compensate for this reduction. In hemolytic anemias, the etiology of premature erythrocyte destruction is diverse and can include intrinsic membrane defects, abnormal hemoglobin, erythrocyte enzymatic defects, immune-mediated destruction of erythrocytes, mechanical injury, and hypersplenism. Hemolysis may also be intramedullary, occurring when fragile red blood cell (RBC) precursors are destroyed in the bone marrow before they are released into circulation. [20] Bone marrow changes also lead to physical obstruction and destruction of the bone marrow microenvironment.

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Pathophysiology
content: Anemia secondary to cancer occurs through common mechanisms: decreased RBC production, increased RBC destruction, blood loss, or other etiologies. However, in some cases, significant anemia has also been observed in the absence of marrow invasion or nutrient deficiency. This suggests that other pathways may be important in the pathogenetic processes leading to anemia, cancer, or marrow changes that cause physical obstruction and destruction of the bone marrow microenvironment. [21]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Histopathology
content: The RBCs' average size and hemoglobin content are within the normal range in typical normocytic normochromic anemia cases. Under microscopic examination, RBCs usually appear similar to normal cells. However, notable variations in cell size and shape may be detectable in some cases, thereby obscuring the normal average values. [22] Bone marrow morphology can help us differentiate various types of anemia: Normal morphology: Secondary anemia (inflammation, renal disease, endocrine deficiency, etc) Hypoplastic: Aplastic anemia Infiltration/fibrosis: Leukemia, myelofibrosis, metastases Dyserythropoietic: Myelodysplasia

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Evaluation
content: The common workup required to diagnose normocytic normochromic anemia includes the following: Complete blood count with differential—repeat if there is an acute drop; rule out any dilutional effect. This is typically observed in a patient receiving a substantial volume of fluids over a short period and is associated with a corresponding decline in other cell lines. MCV and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Evaluation
content: Reticulocyte count must be obtained to determine the pathophysiologic mechanism of anemia. An increased reticulocyte count indicates hemolysis; other evidence of increased RBC destruction, e.g., increased LDH, increased indirect bilirubin, decreased haptoglobin, should also be considered. A decreased reticulocyte count is associated with a hypoproliferative state, such as aplastic anemia, kidney disease, hypothyroidism, etc. Corrected reticulocyte count = percent reticulocytes x (patient's hematocrit/normal hematocrit) Peripheral smear - Erythrocyte morphology (shape and size; absence of schistocytes rules out microangiopathic hemolysis; microspherocytes indicate hemolysis; rouleaux formation relates to multiple myeloma. Lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, bilirubin - to rule out hemolysis Iron panel (iron, ferritin, total iron binding capacity, transferrin saturation) [8]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Evaluation
content: If normocytic normochromic anemia with a secondary cause is suspected, the following tests should be done as per diagnosis/clinical suspicion: Renal failure: BUN/creatinine, erythropoietin level (end-stage renal disease) Autoimmune causes: antinuclear antibody, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and other studies, depending on symptoms and signs Hypothyroidism: Thyroid function tests Multiple myeloma: Serum and urine electrophoresis, serum and urine-free light chains Aplastic anemia: Drug exposure, infections (Epstein-Barr virus, hepatitis, cytomegalovirus, human immunodeficiency virus, parvovirus), hematologic malignancies, and paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria Pure red cell aplasia: Test for parvovirus B19, exclude thymoma [25]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Treatment / Management
content: Management of normocytic, normochromic anemia depends primarily on treating the underlying cause. Blood transfusion remains an important short-term management option, especially in individuals with severe anemia (hemoglobin <7 g/dL), those who are symptomatic, or have associated cardiac disease. [26]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Treatment / Management
content: Anemia of Chronic Disease: Treatment of the anemia of chronic disease requires treating the underlying disorder. Anemia of chronic disease is typically mild, but approximately 20% of patients may have hemoglobin levels <8 g/dL. In these more severe cases, clinicians should rule out additional concurrent causes of anemia, such as iron deficiency anemia. The use of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, blood transfusion, and iron supplementation to treat the underlying diseases is the most important treatment option. If patients have low or inappropriately normal erythropoietin levels, they may respond to erythropoietin or darbepoetin injections. Patients with appropriately elevated EPO levels (especially >500 mU/ML) do not respond. The anemia of chronic disease is often mistaken for iron deficiency anemia. [27] [28] It is crucial to differentiate normocytic normochromic anemia from iron deficiency anemia since iron overload may result in undesirable consequences such as liver necrosis, seizures, cardiogenic shock, and even coma. [29]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Treatment / Management
content: Acute Blood Loss: Treated with efforts to stop bleeding and supportive measures such as IV fluids, cross-matched packed RBC, and oxygen support. Rheumatoid Arthritis: Anti-TNF-α antibodies have been shown to reduce the severity of anemia. [30]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Treatment / Management
content: End-stage Renal Disease (ESRD): Usually due to decreased renal erythropoietin-stimulating agents, the goal hemoglobin is 10.5-11 g/dl in ESRD patients withhemoglobin<10 g/dl. ESRD patients with transferrin saturation ≤30% and ferritin ≤500 ng/ml require iron supplementation, preferably with intravenous rather than oral iron. [31] Primary Bone Marrow Failure: Conditions such as aplastic anemia require immunosuppressive therapy and bone marrow transplantation. [32]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Treatment / Management
content: Hemolytic Anemia: If caused by faulty mechanical valves (macroangiopathic hemolytic anemia), the valves require replacement. Hemolytic anemia caused by medications requires the removal of the offending drug. Hemolytic anemia caused by inherited disorders is treated according to the specific disorder. Persistent hemolytic anemia may require splenectomy. Hemoglobinopathies: Simple blood transfusions, exchange transfusions, and hydroxyurea.

content: Anemia may not be immediately evident on laboratory testing in acute blood loss from trauma, as fluid shifts have less time to normalize circulating volume and dilute the remaining RBCs. title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Prognosis
content: Normocytic normochromic anemia is typically not severe, although it can progress over time and with the evolution of the underlying cause. Prognosis is worse when accompanying certain chronic conditions, such as bone marrow failure, autoimmune conditions, or malignancy. Similarly, the prognosis may be altered by a comorbid condition like coronary artery disease, especially in older patients. Likewise, if treated early, anemia due to acute blood loss has a good prognosis. Mortality rates are low in hemolytic anemias. The etiology of hemolysis and the underlying disorder, such as sickle cell disease or malaria, determine morbidity. In general, the underlying disease is the strongest predictor of prognosis in normocytic, normochromic anemia. [34]

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Complications
content: Most normocytic anemias appear to result from impaired red cell production or erythropoietin deficiency in renal failure. As in the case of anemia associated with chronic infections or systemic diseases, the symptoms are usually associated with those of the underlying condition, although anemia may sometimes be the most prominent sign. Likewise, complications vary according to the underlying disease. These include: Hypoxia (hypoxic respiratory failure, end-organ damage) Renal osteodystrophy (in chronic kidney disease, through secondary hyperparathyroidism) Cardiorenal anemia syndrome: Severe anemia causes a decline in blood perfusion to the kidneys, causing additional kidney damage [35] Cardiovascular disease Multiorgan failure Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly Jaundice

title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Populations at high risk should be considered for interprofessional evaluation. Patients should work with their healthcare provider to treat the underlying disease, address acute conditions like hemorrhage, and adopt healthy habits. title: Normochromic Normocytic Anemia -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The diagnosis and management of normocytic normochromic anemia require an interprofessional team that includes a primary care provider, an internist, and, if relevant, a hematologist, a gastroenterologist, a gynecologist, a surgeon, and a nurse practitioner, as well as other professional teams. The key is to find the underlying disease and, if already diagnosed, treat and manage it. After the diagnosis of the underlying disease, appropriate treatment, in most cases, attenuates the anemia and prevents complications.
